blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — occupational radiation protection during hospitalized brachytherapy care
stem: A nurse provides necessary care to a hospitalized client receiving sealed-source brachytherapy. Which approach best applies basic occupational radiation-protection principles?

options.A: Cluster necessary care to minimize time near the source, maximize distance when care permits, and follow prescribed shielding and radiation-safety instructions.
options.B: Remain close to the bedside to reduce visit frequency, using routine gown and gloves as the primary protection while completing care in one longer session.
options.C: Avoid entering the room until the source is removed unless an emergency occurs, because routine nursing care should be deferred during brachytherapy.
options.D: Increase distance from the source but omit shielding during brief visits, because time and distance provide adequate protection for routine nursing care.

rationale: A is correct. The U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission identifies time, distance, and shielding as core principles for minimizing occupational radiation exposure: limiting exposure time reduces dose, increasing distance markedly decreases radiation intensity and dose, and appropriate shielding reduces exposure to penetrating radiation. NRC regulation 10 CFR §35.410 also requires radiation-safety instruction for personnel caring for certain hospitalized brachytherapy patients, including safe handling and shielding instructions, patient and visitor control, and emergency notification procedures. Therefore necessary nursing care should be performed efficiently while maximizing distance when feasible and following the trained facility radiation-safety/shielding plan. B is incorrect because routine gown and gloves are not substitutes for radiation shielding and remaining unnecessarily close increases exposure. C is incorrect because radiation protection does not require withholding necessary nursing care; care is provided using trained safety controls. D is incorrect because time, distance, and shielding are complementary protection principles and brief exposure does not justify disregarding prescribed shielding instructions.
educational_objective: Minimize occupational radiation exposure during hospitalized brachytherapy care by limiting time near the source, maximizing distance when feasible, and following prescribed shielding and radiation-safety instructions while continuing necessary care.
source_organization: U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC); National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)

source_locator: NRC 'Minimize Your Exposure' lines 26-40: time, distance and shielding minimize radiation exposure; minimizing time reduces dose, increasing distance reduces intensity/dose, and proper shielding reduces penetrating-radiation exposure. NRC 10 CFR §35.410 lines 155-173: personnel caring for brachytherapy patients who cannot be released under §35.75 must receive radiation-safety instruction commensurate with duties, including source appearance, safe handling and shielding, patient control, visitor control, and emergency notification to the Radiation Safety Officer/designee and authorized user. NCSBN 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan Safety and Infection Prevention and Control page was visually verified earlier in this continuation and supports environmental-hazard protection and safe equipment/procedure use.
source_claim_supported: Fresh current NRC HTML directly supports time, distance and shielding as complementary exposure-minimization principles and confirms that brachytherapy-care personnel receive safe-handling/shielding instructions. The final item does not assert that all sealed-source brachytherapy patients are regulated identically or prescribe one universal room configuration; it tests portable occupational-safety principles plus adherence to the trained facility plan. NCSBN supports the environmental-safety blueprint construct.

pdf_visual_verification: PASS — the official 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan Safety and Infection Prevention and Control page was freshly screenshot-verified earlier in this continuation on 2026-08-20. NRC evidence used for Q0213 is current HTML/CFR text; no NRC PDF evidence is relied on.
correction_summary: Original Q0213 had a uniquely longest correct answer, an absolute-word distractor, and alternatives that were easy to reject. The item was rebuilt with four plausible radiation-safety strategies of similar length. The final key integrates all three NRC protection principles and facility-specific shielding instruction without claiming that routine barrier PPE provides radiation shielding or that necessary nursing care should be withheld.

option_audit.A: Correct; directly applies NRC time, distance, and shielding principles and trained brachytherapy safety instructions while preserving necessary care.
option_audit.B: Plausible visit-clustering misconception; incorrect because unnecessary proximity increases exposure and routine gown/gloves are not equivalent to radiation shielding.
option_audit.C: Plausible exposure-avoidance overcorrection; incorrect because necessary care is provided using radiation-safety controls rather than withheld until source removal.
option_audit.D: Plausible partial-ALARA strategy; incorrect because increasing distance does not justify omitting prescribed shielding and safety instructions.

cueing_audit.absolute_words: No option relies on all/only/always/never/must-type absolute wording.
cueing_audit.answer_length: Final option lengths: A 160, B 155, C 149, D 153 characters; the correct answer is not isolated by a large length difference and all options contain comparable safety rationales.
cueing_audit.grammatical_lexical: All four alternatives describe credible ways a nurse might try to reduce radiation exposure and differ in use of time, distance, shielding, or care avoidance rather than obvious tone.
cueing_audit.second_answer_risk: No defensible second answer identified in the pre-stage audit. B substitutes routine PPE for shielding and increases proximity, C withholds necessary care, and D omits one of the three complementary protection principles. Post-fetch adversarial reread remains required.
